analysis.one_liner: Taxes fossil fuels to fund a cut in Social Security payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Ways and Means Committee from May 2009 until the 111th Congress ended with no cosponsors beyond its three original sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a tax on coal, oil, and natural gas — starting at $15 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2010 and rising each year to $100 by 2040, adjusted for inflation. Every dollar collected would go into the Social Security trust funds, and the Treasury Secretary would cut Social Security payroll tax rates by an amount that keeps the trust funds whole — so workers' take-home pay would rise while the same money funded Social Security from a different source. It would also tax certain carbon-heavy imports so U.S. manufacturers would not be undercut, and it would make a one-time extra payment to Social Security beneficiaries in 2010 to cover the higher energy prices before those prices worked into their cost-of-living adjustment. The bill locked in revenue neutrality: any attempt to raise the carbon tax beyond what the payroll cut needed would require a two-thirds vote in the House or Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people would gain the most: cutting the employee and employer Social Security payroll tax rates raises take-home pay and reduces a tax on hiring. Social Security beneficiaries would be protected — the trust funds would receive the carbon tax revenue in place of the payroll taxes, and 2010 recipients would get a one-time payment covering the carbon tax's effect on prices. Domestic manufacturers in carbon-intensive industries would gain from the border tax on competing imports.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payroll taxpayers and Social Security recipients

how_it_helps.text: The Social Security payroll tax rate would be cut each year by a percentage calculated to offset exactly the revenue raised by the new carbon tax, keeping the trust funds whole [S3] [S2].
Social Security beneficiaries would receive a one-time increase in 2010 payments to cover the average cost of the carbon tax before it is reflected in cost-of-living adjustments [S3].
All net carbon tax revenue would be appropriated to the Social Security trust funds in the same proportions as ordinary payroll tax receipts [S3] [S2].

Certain imports from industries that use large amounts of carbon-based energy would be taxed at the same rate as domestic production, so the tax would not simply push manufacturing overseas [S3] [S2].
Businesses that capture or sequester carbon instead of emitting it could claim a refund of the tax, and exports would be exempt, keeping U.S. exporters from paying the tax on goods sold abroad [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal, petroleum, and natural gas producers and importers would owe the tax, and they would pass much of it to consumers through higher prices for gasoline, electricity, heating fuel, and goods made with those fuels. The bill's one-time 2010 payment to beneficiaries covers only that first year; after 2010, people outside the workforce who pay no payroll tax would absorb higher energy prices with no offset.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The carbon tax would be passed through to consumers as higher prices for gasoline, electricity, and heating, and the bill's protection for those price increases is a single one-time payment to Social Security beneficiaries in 2010 only [S3].
The payroll tax cut helps workers, but people who are retired or otherwise not on payroll would face the higher energy prices with no offset after 2010 [S3].

The bill requires a two-thirds vote in either chamber to raise the carbon tax beyond revenue-neutrality, making it much harder for a future Congress to use the revenue for anything other than the payroll tax cut [S3] [S2].
The payroll cut and the tax are linked only by Treasury estimates, so if carbon tax revenue falls short, adjustments would be needed after the fact [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is a swap that works in workers' favor: it replaces a direct tax on wages with a tax on fossil fuels, and it protects Social Security's financing rather than cutting benefits. The serious weakness is on the other side of the ledger for people who pay no payroll tax — after the one-year 2010 payment, retirees and others would eat the higher energy prices without any offset, and the supermajority lock would make it hard to redirect revenue to fix that. Whether the trade is good depends heavily on how the rising tax (from $15 to $100 per ton over 30 years) filters into prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules Committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Inglis (R-SC) introduced the bill on May 13, 2009, joined by Reps. Daniel Lipinski (D-IL) and Jeff Flake (R-AZ) [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the House Rules Committee the same day [S5] [S1].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 111th Congress [S5].
Only two additional members cosponsored the bill, one Democrat and one Republican, out of 431 voting members of the House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas producers came out ahead: a tax that would have started at $15 per ton of carbon dioxide and climbed to $100 never took effect. Workers got neither the payroll tax cut nor the higher energy prices, so the deal that would have traded one for the other simply never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; no one got the payroll cut

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — two Republicans and one Democrat — but the bill attracted only one more cosponsor from each party and never reached a vote, so no party-position roll call exists; the outcome was committee inaction rather than a party split.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill taxes every ton of coal, petroleum product, and natural gas extracted, produced, or imported, at a rate rising from $15 to $100 per ton of carbon dioxide by 2040. Their interest in the bill was to keep the tax off the books; the public's interest was the payroll tax cut and lower emissions funded by it.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive importers and retailers of fuel and power
industries.note: Importers of carbon-heavy products would owe the tax at the border, and utilities and refiners would pass the fuel tax through to household bills. The public paid in higher energy prices but got a payroll tax cut and a one-time benefit payment in return.
A border tax on competing imports from the highest-carbon industries would shield domestic producers from cheaper foreign goods made with untaxed energy.

industries.industry: Social Security trust funds and beneficiaries
industries.note: The funds would keep receiving the same money, from carbon tax revenue instead of payroll taxes, and beneficiaries would get a one-time 2010 payment for the price impact — but after that first year the tax's price effects hit people with no payroll tax cut to offset them.
